abstract: Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. Project website: https://anonymousprojects-dev.github.io/LLM-guided-LocoManipulation-Quadrupeds/

title: Reaction precedents extend retrosynthetic prediction beyond training coverage
abstract: Reaction precedents guide retrosynthesis, but how far they can compensate for gaps in task-specific training coverage remains unclear. Using 2.71 million reactions, we restricted training and retrieval coverage by transformation or time, then expanded only the retrieval corpus with model parameters fixed. For transformations excluded from training, mean Top-1 accuracy increased from 13.0% to 58.0% on a historical test set and from 4.9% to 23.1% on a temporally held-out test set. For temporal coverage gaps, retrieval expansion enabled a model trained on records before 2017 to match or exceed a non-retrieval model trained on records before 2025 on both test sets. Without task-specific fine-tuning, precedents improved all 14 representative general-purpose models on both test sets and USPTO-50K; the strongest with precedents surpassed all eight representative specialized models. These findings show that inference-time reaction precedents can extend retrosynthetic prediction beyond task-specific training coverage without parameter updates.

title: Distributional Reward Calibration and Budget-Neutral Credit Assignment for Multimodal RLVR
abstract: We revisit advantage estimation in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and observe that any token-level advantage admits a two-stage factorization: a \emph{sample-level baselining} step that converts scalar verifier rewards into a comparable sequence-level signal, and a \emph{token-level credit assignment} step that distributes that signal over the trajectory. Existing estimators typically address only one of these stages: affine baselines preserve the shape of each task's reward law, so heavy tails and binary cliffs propagate into the gradient, while token-level credit rules tie the size of each token's update to raw confidence scales and need not conserve the total credit issued by the verifier. We propose \textbf{TACE} (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a two-stage estimator that addresses both stages. At stage~(S1), we replace linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal, which gives a common population reward law across tasks and caps finite-sample outliers deterministically. At stage~(S2), we rank-calibrate a stop-gradient evidence contrast within each trajectory and renormalize the clipped token weights to have mean one, so credit is redistributed across tokens while its total mass and sign are conserved. We prove population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. On a multimodal reasoning suite, TACE obtains the strongest results on a majority of the benchmarks but does not dominate every setting.

title: Chiral superconductivity on a closed Klein bottle: a chirality wall and its Majorana seam spectrum
abstract: We study a spinless $π$-flux lattice superconductor whose normal-state momentum-space fundamental domain is a Klein bottle. Within this model, a glide lift and a hidden antiunitary symmetry independently force the Bogoliubov--de Gennes (BdG) Chern number to vanish. A diagonal pairing breaks the antiunitary obstruction exactly when its real part is nonzero; this is necessary, not sufficient, for a chiral phase. We derive explicit Pfaffians determining Chern parity and identify three analytic families of gap closings in a real-pairing section. For a chiral state on a closed real-space Klein bottle, the prescribed pairing and gluing produce a $ΔC=2$ chirality wall. A translation-invariant unfolding resolves two co-propagating Majorana branches. Their finite-size levels depend on circumference and holonomy; the near-zero pair is lifted at first order by allowed local seam perturbations. A cut-cylinder control has the same low-energy channel count, so gluing reconnects existing gapless content. We also distinguish literal gluing from deck projection: particle--hole symmetry exchanges the deck eigenblocks, precluding their interpretation as independent BdG quotient Hamiltonians. The contribution is a model-specific account of pairing compatibility and closed-surface seam spectra. The energy cost is evaluated for a fixed pairing background; neither a protected zero mode nor a self-consistent wall solution is claimed.

title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.

title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.

title: Statistical Analysis of Synthetic Data with Verification: A Linear Regression Framework
abstract: Synthetic data are widely used for training modern AI systems. However, their statistical understanding remains limited. It is well recognized in statistics that repeated self-training on synthetic data can amplify errors inherited from pre-trained models, leading to model collapse. Verification plays a crucial role in selecting high-quality synthetic data to help prevent model collapse and improve model performance. We study verified self-training in a linear regression framework, where a pre-trained estimator generates synthetic data with injected generation noise and a verifier selects samples according to a verification threshold. Post-training on the accepted samples updates either all coordinates (full fine-tuning) or only an active subset (partial fine-tuning). Our analysis reveals three potentially counterintuitive effects. We establish that tighter verification does not always lead to lower prediction risk. We also find that a suitable level of injected generation noise can reduce prediction risk, while excessive noise can increase it. Moreover, full and partial fine-tuning can respond differently to the same verification rule, since pre-training error in the frozen coordinates affects both sample selection and post-training risk. We analyze these effects by deriving finite sample risk bounds for four separate regimes determined by the relative scales of the verification threshold, generation noise, and pre-training error. The bounds precisely characterize how verification affects prediction risk across these regimes. In particular, we quantify how the generation noise, the effective accepted sample size, and the covariance of the accepted covariates affect prediction risk. The analysis extends to iterative verified full fine-tuning, where sufficiently tight verification reduces the initial error contribution at a geometric rate.

title: A Candidate Binary Microlensing Event in the 2018 Gamma-Ray Flare of 3C 279
abstract: The April 2018 gamma-ray flare of the flat-spectrum radio quasar 3C~279 exhibited sharp peaks within a broader outburst. Its rapid substructure was previously attributed to magnetic reconnection. Motivated by its distinctive temporal profile within our comparison sample of bright blazar flares and its resemblance to caustic-crossing features in optical microlensing events, we investigate a finite-source binary-microlensing interpretation. A jointly fitted model of binary-lens magnification, a smooth intrinsic flare, and Gaussian-process variability reproduces the principal double-peaked structure of the GeV light curve. The adopted local solution has a binary mass ratio of $q\simeq0.098$ and an Einstein timescale of $t_{\rm E}\simeq0.327$~d. The absolute lens mass and projected source radius depend on the lens distance and relative proper motion. The fitted geometry can correspond to a Galactic planetary-mass binary or an intervening stellar or substellar system, with different physical source sizes in each case. We present binary microlensing as a testable interpretation of this event, with the finite-source structure offering a potential probe of the compact GeV-emitting region.

title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
abstract: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.

title: Learned Terminal Costs for Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control of Autonomous Trucks in Interactive Highway Traffic
abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.

title: Reframing Spatial Uncertainty Visualisation with a Layered Grammar of Graphics
abstract: Communicating both estimated values and their associated uncertainties presents a particular challenge in spatial visualisation because spatial coordinates already occupy the primary visual channels, leaving relatively few channels available for encoding uncertainty alongside the estimated values. A range of visualisation techniques has been developed to address this challenge, including bivariate choropleth maps, pixel maps, and glyph maps. However, existing implementations typically treat these techniques as dedicated visualisations rather than expressing them through the composable elements of a grammar of graphics. We reframe uncertainty visualisation as an extension of the layered grammar of graphics, allowing uncertainty-specific representations to be composed, customised, and extended alongside other graphical components. We demonstrate this perspective by integrating uncertainty visualisation into the layered architecture of ggplot2, accommodating these techniques while also motivating new approaches such as the dual map for selective attention between estimated values and their associated uncertainties. We implement the framework in the R package ggincerta and demonstrate its application through three case studies.

title: The Price of a Chance in Artificial Societies
abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous agents to interact, coordinate, and pursue individual goals in artificial societies. However, our understanding of how reward structures shape their competitive behavior and collective outcomes remains incomplete. We simulate 200 LLM agents competing over 50 rounds to maximize individual wealth. We define overcompetition and lying flat as population investment above and below a Bayesian adaptive baseline, respectively. At the lowest tested reward, populations lie flat; at the two highest, they overcompete, most strongly at intermediate winner coverage. The investment committed to pursuing an uncertain reward constitutes the price of a chance. Agents near the qualification cutoff can invest heavily yet receive no prize, finishing poorer than nonwinners who invest less. Agents' stated rationales link investment decisions to perceived qualification prospects and expected returns. At the collective level, greater investment does not consistently improve ability selection. With a fixed total prize budget, offering smaller prizes to more winners can reduce investment while preserving selection quality relative to the corresponding top-ability target. Further broadening reward coverage yields additional savings but reduces selection quality. These findings show how reward design shapes overcompetition and lying flat, distributes the costs of pursuing opportunity, and influences what competition collectively achieves.

title: Unweaving the mechanics of woven fabrics through automated model discovery
abstract: Woven fabrics have multiple structural, aesthetic, and medical applications that require knowledge of their mechanical properties. While isolated fiber properties are easily determined, bulk properties of woven material, which can be coated or locally reinforced, require knowledge of yarn density, weave style, and other characteristics that are difficult to obtain experimentally. Additionally, fiber rearrangement, twist, yarn contact, and fiber-direction coupling result in non-linear mechanical responses. As a result, there is no universal material model for woven materials, and each fabric requires a specific model and parameter calibration. Recently, methods to simultaneously discover material models and their parameters from experimental or synthetic datasets have been proposed. Here, we use automated model discovery to simultaneously extract the material model and its parameters from biaxial test data of a TPU-coated woven nylon fabric. We show that Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks discover a sparse three-term hyperelastic material law with one isotropic and two anisotropic contributions, reproducing the measured biaxial response with a mean $R^2=0.97$. Across 20 initializations, predictive accuracy remains robust despite variations in the exact sparse representation, consistent with strong correlations between several candidate terms. LARS-LASSO independently recovers the same dominant constitutive contributions at approximately 100-fold lower computational cost. These results are directly applicable to numerical finite-element models of fabric-based structures, including soft robotic devices. More broadly, these results provide a foundation for further model discovery, improved constitutive modeling, and mechanistically informed optimization of woven fabric structures.

title: An Arithmetic Property of Intertwining Operators for Real Reductive Groups
abstract: Let $G$ be the group of complex points of a connected split reductive group defined over ${\mathbb Q}$. We study the standard intertwining operator between representations parabolically induced from essentially tempered cohomological representations of Levi subgroups of maximal parabolic subgroups. Under certain algebraicity, purity, and criticality hypotheses, the operator is holomorphic and invertible at a particular point of evaluation. The relative Lie algebra cohomology of these induced representations is one-dimensional in the lowest nonzero degree. Under prescribed rational generators of these one-dimensional spaces, we show that the intertwining operator is a nonzero rational multiple of a certain product of ratios of local $L$-factors. This is a cohomological version of Langlands's calculation of the Gindikin-Karplevic formula. The main theorem provides a local input for the arithmetic study of special values of Langlands--Shahidi $L$-functions.

title: PCR-ALERA: A PCR-ELISA analogue but antibody-free DNA detection system
abstract: PCR-ALERA is a new concept for DNA detection that combines DNA amplification by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with an activator-linked enzyme reactivation assay (ALERA). PCR-ALERA resembles the commercial, semi-quantitative PCR-ELISA assay that offers high sensitivity and high-throughput screening in microplates. PCR-ALERA overcomes a major drawback of PCR-ELISA since it does not require the time-consuming handling of expensive antibodies. In the first step of the assay, commercially available modified nucleotides were incorporated during PCR amplification of the target DNA. A selenocysteine containing peptide (the activator) was linked to the amplified DNA by click chemistry. This peptide has been optimized for the highly efficient activation of the latent protease papain by selenolate-triggered disulfide cleavage. The DNA-peptide hybrid was then immoblized in microplate wells and incubated with latent papain. The latter was readily activated and converted a fluorogenic substrate to a fluorescent product with high catalytic turnover. Overall assay time is about 4 hours including PCR.

title: Heavy-Particle Effective Theory: from On-Shell Formalism to Gravitational Compton Amplitudes
abstract: We formulate on-shell heavy-particle effective theory (HPET) amplitudes by projecting the spinor-helicity variables onto the $SU(2)$ little group of a timelike reference velocity $v^μ$. Retaining both large and small components of the velocity-projected spinors gives an intermediate velocity-projected amplitudes in which reparameterization invariance can be imposed before expanding in the inverse heavy-particle mass. Integrating out the small component then yields HPET amplitudes organized by heavy-particle power counting, with a direct correspondence to local operators at fixed order. We determine the three-point velocity-projected amplitudes for two equal-mass particles of arbitrary spin $S$ coupled to a soft massless boson of helicity $h$. Four-point gravitational Compton amplitudes can be constructively obtained using velocity-projected three-point amplitudes, and expanded into HPET amplitudes which is free of spurious poles up to sub-leading order. As a gravitational application, we show that the projected gravitational minimal coupling reproduces the Kerr spin-induced multipoles up to order $2S$, and find the classical limits of the tree-level elastic gravitational scattering and gravitational Compton amplitudes agreed with the literature up to contact terms undetermined by factorization.

title: From MS/MS evidence to adaptive spectroscopic characterization: Reinforcement learning guided by candidate molecular structures
abstract: Small-molecule identification from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) may require complementary measurements. Herein, we propose a structure-informed deep Q-network (SI-DQN) that uses existing MS/MS evidence to decide whether further characterization is needed, which measurement to request, and when to stop. The policy combines spectral representations and candidate rankings with score-weighted descriptors of the candidates' chemical features and structural differences. The policy was evaluated on 79,462 held-out samples with simulated MS/MS, infrared (IR), and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra from the Multimodal Spectroscopic Dataset. Evaluation used fixed hard candidate sets containing the correct structure and equal normalized acquisition costs. Averaged across three training runs, SI-DQN increased Top-1 accuracy from 80.10% to 93.78% for positive-ion MS/MS starts and from 70.44% to 93.31% for negative-ion starts. The corresponding mean additional measurement counts were only 0.227 and 0.340 per sample, respectively. Complete acquisition achieved 97.72% accuracy with four additions, whereas SI-DQN reduced the additional measurement count by 94.3% and 91.5%. Relative to a rule-based policy, SI-DQN reduced the composite loss combining terminal ranking error and acquisition cost by 19.3% and 25.5%. Adding structural information to DQN further improved accuracy while reducing requests across all three training runs. At comparable ranking uncertainty, SI-DQN increased request rates relative to DQN more strongly in groups with high structural disagreement, where larger reductions in composite loss were also observed. Together, these results support using the ambiguity among candidate structures after MS/MS analysis to guide further characterization, providing a quantitative basis for balancing identification performance against subsequent measurement effort.

title: Division and noetherianity in quasianalytic Denjoy-Carleman classes
abstract: We show that the local rings of quasianalytic Denjoy-Carleman classes need not be Noetherian. More precisely, we construct quasianalytic Denjoy-Carleman classes $C^M$ whose local rings $C^M(\mathbb{R}^d,0)$ are not Noetherian for any $d\geq 2$. Conversely, we exhibit quasianalytic classes whose local rings in dimension two are regular and Noetherian. Our approach is based on the problem of exact division: if $f=φg$, where $f\in C^M$, $φ$ is real-analytic, and $g\in C^\infty$, under which conditions does it follow that $g\in C^M$? We introduce a quantitative scale-growth condition on the defining weight sequence $M$ and prove that exact division holds in two variables whenever this condition is sufficiently strong relative to the rate at which the nonreal branches of the complex zero set of $φ$ approach the real plane. We also construct quasianalytic weight sequences with prescribed growth thresholds and establish corresponding counterexamples to exact division. These yield nonclosed principal ideals and, consequently, non-Noetherian local rings.

title: Two-loop QCD contribution to the quark-initiated production of a top-antitop quark pair and a Higgs boson at the LHC
abstract: We present the first direct computation of the two-loop QCD virtual corrections to the production of a top-antitop quark pair in association with a Higgs boson ($t\bar{t}H$) at the LHC. We focus on the quark-antiquark channel and perform the calculation in the generalised leading-colour approximation. We combine state-of-the-art numerical methods for multiloop calculations with machine learning techniques to construct a surrogate amplitude suitable for accurate cross section computations. We compare our numerical results with those previously obtained using dynamical approximations of the two-loop amplitude, finding agreement within their respective uncertainties.

title: Extreme values of Artin $L$-functions at $s=1$
abstract: Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a Galois extension of number fields with Galois group $G$. Let $χ$ be any character on $G$ and $κ(χ)$ be the leading coefficient of the Laurent series of the Artin $L$-function $L(s,χ)$ at $s=1$. Cho, Lemke Oliver, and Zaman (2026) recently established a conditional bound for $κ(χ)$ assuming GRH for the Dedekind zeta function of $K$. Up to implied constants, we show that the extremal values of these bounds are attained for an infinite family of extensions $K/\mathbb{Q}$ and all irreducible faithful characters $χ$, provided $G$ is a regular Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$. All characters $χ$ are permitted without restriction when $G$ is abelian, $A_n, S_n$, or any sporadic group. Our method removes the assumptions of GRH and Artin's holomorphy conjecture from an argument of Duke (2003) by following the strategy of Lemke Oliver, Thorner, and Zaman (2024) on the existence of extremal class numbers for number fields of arbitrary degree. Key ingredients include progress by Débes (2017) towards Malle's conjecture, and an Artin $L$-function large sieve by Lemke Oliver and Smith (2024).

title: Probabilistic Energy-Based Neural Networks for Uncertainty-Aware Collider Data Analyses
abstract: We introduce a probabilistic energy-based Neural Network (NN) for uncertainty-aware classification in collider analyses. Standard discriminative classifiers can give highly confident predictions even for events that are different from the data used during training. Energy-Based Models provide an alternative by assigning an energy score to each event, which measures how well the event agrees with the learned data distribution. In this framework, a NN maps the input features into a latent space, where the energy is defined with respect to class-specific embeddings. This allows the model to identify noisy, anomalous or shifted events while maintaining good classification performance. We first study the method using controlled synthetic examples and then test it in a realistic collider analysis based on the $h \to τ^+ τ^-$ process at the Large Hadron Collider, where $h$ is the discovered Standard Model Higgs boson. We show that the associated energy score can help identify events affected by mismodelling and/or systematic variations and can thus be used to define uncertainty-aware event selections. Although we use this specific Higgs process as a testbed, the method is general and can be applied to other collider classification problems where robustness against systematic and distributional uncertainties is important.

title: When Modernization Breaks Working Code: A Single-File Study of LLMs on Legacy PHP
abstract: Pasting a legacy file into an LLM and asking it to "modernize this" is an easy shortcut. But is the result better than leaving the code alone? In this paper, we study this single-file setting with five LLMs, each asked to modernize 100 WordPress 4.0 PHP files to PHP 8.3 while preserving behavior, with no project context or execution feedback. We evaluate every output with 630 hidden behavioral checks and 511 Rector-detected modernization findings. We compare against two baselines: the unchanged originals and the rule-based tool Rector. Often, the answer is no. Untouched, 83 files already pass every check; the best LLM leaves only 59. Each model breaks 32-51 working files while repairing at most 10, whereas Rector breaks 7 and repairs 6. Most of this damage is unnecessary. Only 37 findings (7 percent) require a change under PHP 8.3, yet in compatible files with no required change, the LLMs break 36-60 percent (Rector: 8 percent). The model with the highest modernization score is no more compatible than its closest competitors. Most regressed checks come from files that no longer load at all, often because of type declarations PHP itself rejects. These are errors that need no project context to avoid. Evaluations of LLM-based modernization should therefore measure against a no-change baseline and report modernization and behavioral preservation separately.

title: On separators in $K_t$-minor-free graphs
abstract: This manuscript presents a proof of the Alon--Seymour--Thomas conjecture developed under the author's guidance using ChatGPT 6pro. The author has checked every formula and theorem by hand and used Codex to assist with writing. GPT 6.1 Sol (Max) was also used to check the proof repeatedly and to generate numerous examples for verification. More precisely, for every integer $h\geq3$, every $n$-vertex $K_h$-minor-free graph has a vertex set of size at most $\min{n,21h\sqrt n}$ whose deletion leaves every component with at most $2n/3$ vertices.

title: Gaussian Distillation of Flow Policies
abstract: Flow policies are among the strongest robot controllers and are well suited to modelling multimodal action distributions. Our analysis shows that the continuous-action distributions of the studied flow policies are well approximated by Gaussians. We propose the Gaussian Action Readout (GAR), which replaces a flow policy's final layer with a Gaussian readout trained on just 0.02% of eligible states, while keeping the rest of the network frozen. It samples with one action-network pass, gives closed-form likelihoods, and achieves near-teacher task success at up to twice the inference speed.

title: posterior-landscape: morphological feature finding in two-dimensional probability densities
abstract: We present posterior-landscape, a Python framework to identify and characterize morphological features in two-dimensional probability densities. The framework combines concepts from topological data analysis, statistical density-ridge estimation, and scale-space image analysis. It extracts localized concentrations, valleys, ridges, and changes of slope; for Bayesian reconstructions, it propagates uncertainty in feature recovery, geometry, and correspondence across posteriors. The framework also connects two-dimensional structures to features in one-dimensional marginals, and quantifies their correlation with other inferred parameters. We validate the method on controlled densities, and demonstrate its use on gravitational-wave population reconstructions, where it provides a systematic way to identify and interpret population features and assess which ones carry information relevant for cosmology. The resulting catalogues also offer a common morphological representation for future comparisons between predictions and population reconstructions.

title: Bounds for General $(r,δ)$-Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes
abstract: We study general $(r,δ)$-quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) without assuming purity or a stabilizer structure, and with arbitrarily overlapping recovery blocks. Using a selection lemma for multiple-erasure recovery, we establish a Singleton-like upper bound for general quantum subspaces. When $δ=2$, this bound reduces to the general single-erasure bound of Golowich and Guruswami. An integer optimization yields an explicit remainder correction that tightens the bound by up to $δ-2$. For pure codes, local decoupling and entropy arguments extend the parameter bound of Galindo et al., originally obtained for pure stabilizer codes constructed from Euclidean or Hermitian dual-containing classical codes, to arbitrary pure quantum subspaces. We also remove the partition assumption from several existing pure-code bounds for disjoint recovery blocks and obtain a further remainder correction by optimizing the budget. Finally, we analyze three families attaining these bounds: pure codes with overlapping recovery blocks and $d=δ$, which exhibit both a strict improvement of the pure-code bound and simultaneous equality in the pure-code and general bounds; impure codes with disjoint recovery blocks attaining the general bound; and an existing family of pure codes with overlapping recovery blocks and $d>δ$, which simultaneously attains all these bounds.

title: $\mathcal{N}=2$ conformal higher-spin actions in harmonic superspace
abstract: We construct linearized $4D, \mathcal{N}=2$ Weyl-type off-shell actions in harmonic superspace for the superconformal higher-spin gauge multiplets introduced in arXiv:2404.19016. This work is a followup of our arXiv:2511.16325, where an analogous construction was carried out for conformal $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity. We check the superconformal invariance of the new actions and their linearized gauge invariance. As the characteristic features of our formulation, the structure of the underlying prepotentials and their gauge and superconformal transformations are entirely determined by the fundamental \textit{principle of Grassmann harmonic analyticity}, while the construction of the invariant actions and of the generalized $\mathcal{N}=2$ super-Weyl tensors relies upon the \textit{principle of Grassmann half-analyticity}. This provides not only a new geometric framework for the linearized $\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal gauge higher-spin theories, but also suggests possible ways of promoting them to the full nonlinear level. We consider a generalization to an arbitrary $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity background and show that the linearized spin-$\mathbf{s}$ gauge invariance, without radical modifications of the gauge transformation law and/or harmonic zero-curvature equations, is consistent only with $\mathcal{N}=2$ Weyl-flat super-backgrounds.

title: Going off the (momentum) grid: A simple implementation of noncold relics in linear Boltzmann solvers
abstract: Linear Boltzmann solvers typically evolve the perturbations of noncold relics, such as massive neutrinos or hot subcomponents of the dark matter, on a momentum grid, often switching to a fluid approximation on small scales for efficiency. We implement in CLASS the Dispersive Fluid Approximation (DFA), a fluid scheme that captures the scale-dependent sound speed of these species. Within the standard ncdm module, the DFA significantly outperforms the default CLASS fluid approximation in the cross and neutrino power spectra, and reduces errors in the cold dark matter power spectrum by up to an order of magnitude, while adding only 1-4% to the total runtime. We also present the first open-source implementation of the Generalized Boltzmann Hierarchy (GBH), which simplifies the implementation of noncold relics by integrating out the momentum dependence of their perturbations altogether. Combined with the DFA and tested on massive neutrinos, the GBH reproduces the matter power spectrum to better than permille accuracy and cosmological parameter constraints to better than 0.05 sigma, at a computational cost comparable to that of the standard implementation. We argue that the GBH is particularly well suited to non-thermal relics whose distribution function varies with time or across parameter space. Our implementation of both the DFA and the GBH in CLASS is publicly available at https://github.com/aradn97/class_GBH.

title: TaskFrame: Connecting Task-Level Planning with Frame-Level Control for Game Agents
abstract: Building general game agents requires both high-level task reasoning and low-latency action control in rapidly changing visual environments. These capabilities favor models with substantially different computational profiles, making them difficult to realize within a single model. In this work, we present TaskFrame, a hierarchical planner-controller framework that connects task-level planning with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control. A vision-language task planner decomposes a high-level goal into an ordered sequence of atomic instructions and is optimized through supervised learning and dependency-aware GRPO. The hidden states of special goal tokens that terminate each atomic instruction provide continuous goal embeddings that are cached and reused across control steps. A causal Transformer controller combines the embedding of the active goal with recent observations to predict discrete keyboard and mouse-button actions and continuous camera motion at every game step. We train the system in three stages: planner training, controller pretraining, and joint alignment. Experiments in Minecraft show that TaskFrame is competitive with general-purpose vision-language models on instruction decomposition, and that in closed-loop evaluation the agent achieves a higher combat success rate than the evaluated baselines.

title: Towards fNIRS foundation models: A curated corpus of 67 public datasets with channel positions in MNI space
abstract: Brain foundation models have transformed medical artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience by reducing the reliance on task-specific data through large-scale pretraining. While they have been successful with non-invasive neuroimaging data, their adoption in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has lagged due to the limited size and heterogeneity of public datasets, which are collected under varying protocols, devices, and sensor configurations. In addition, no single fNIRS dataset is comparable in size to the largest datasets in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). The fNIRS datasets are also spread across different platforms and often have insufficient information, or lack the protocols that would make them easier to use. Given the advances in EEG foundation models that enable flexible modeling across diverse EEG montages, we curated 1,955 hours of fNIRS data from 67 public datasets spanning 2,798 participants, representing the largest fNIRS curation effort to date. The curated data include oxygenated (HbO) and deoxygenated (HbR) hemoglobin signals along with the three-dimensional position of every channel in the standard space of the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI), which makes positions comparable across datasets. We release dataloaders that handle each dataset automatically, along with the minimal preprocessing pipeline used to prepare the data, at https://github.com/sposso/fnirs-datasets. This work aims to facilitate the future development of foundation models for fNIRS.

title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.

title: The Borodin--Kostochka Conjecture for Two Classes of Diamond-Free Graphs
abstract: We prove the Borodin--Kostochka conjecture for $(\mathrm{diamond},L_4)$-free graphs and $(\mathrm{diamond},K_5^+)$-free graphs, where $L_4$ is obtained from $K_4$ by attaching a path of length two to one clique vertex, and $K_5^+$ is obtained from $K_5$ by adding a vertex adjacent to exactly one clique vertex. The proof uses structural properties of maximum cliques in diamond-free vertex-critical graphs with $χ=Δ$.

title: Latent Prediction Yields Cross-Subject Alignable Representations in Sensory-Evoked fMRI
abstract: Decoding sensory-evoked functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data is a central analytical tool in cognitive neuroscience. Here we ask whether self-supervised learning (SSL), which has been scarcely explored in this domain, can yield representations that support strong downstream performance. To do so, we adapt a joint embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to train participant-specific encoders on brain data alone. The encoders never see the stimulus images or any representation derived from them. Applied to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we evaluate our learned brain embeddings on the downstream tasks of brain captioning and image reconstruction, as well as cross-participant generalization. Our self-supervised approach achieves competitive performance with parameter-rich supervised pipelines that are trained end-to-end with access to image and language data. We further find that encoders trained independently for different participants can be aligned fully unsupervised, using neither images nor stimuli shared between them. After alignment, a neural decoding head trained on one participant can be applied to another without fine-tuning and retains most of its within-subject performance on image reconstruction and brain captioning. By removing the need for images and shared stimuli, our approach is a step towards pooling fMRI data across participants and, eventually, across datasets.

title: Layering and reverse extension for weighted $k$-path vertex cover
abstract: We study the weighted $k$-path vertex cover problem for any fixed integer $k \ge 2$, in which a vertex non-negatively weighted simple graph $G = (V, E)$ is given and one wants to find a minimum-weight vertex subset $C \subseteq V$ such that every simple path on $k$ vertices in $G$ contains at least one vertex of $C$. The problem generalizes the classic weighted vertex cover problem, that is, $k = 2$, and it admits a $k$-approximation algorithm of Hochbaum~[SIAM J. Comput., 1982] and a $(k - \frac 12)$-approximation algorithm of Brüstle et al.~[IWOCA 2021]. In this paper, we carefully design local weight functions in the Layering and Reverse Extension local ratio framework of Bar-Yehuda et al.~[ACM Comput. Surv., 2004], leading to an approximation algorithm of ratio $\frac {3k-1}4$ for odd $k \ge 3$ and of ratio $\frac {3k}4$ for even $k \ge 4$. When $k = 3$ and $k = 4$, these ratios are $2$ and $3$, respectively, matching the state-of-the-art approximation ratios for the corresponding special cases.

title: First search for sidereal and annual modulation of $Z$-pole asymmetries with the recovered SLD data set
abstract: We report what is, to our knowledge, the first time-resolved analysis of electroweak asymmetries at the $Z$ pole, using the public release of the recovered SLD collision data: $6.6\times10^5$ polarized $e^+e^-\to Z$ events from the 1996-1998 SLC runs, with 385583 selected hadronic $Z$ decays spanning 782 sidereal cycles. The left-right asymmetry $A_{LR}$, reconstructed with the published SLD selection and per-event signed Compton polarization, shows no sidereal, solar-diurnal, or annual modulation; a simultaneous unbinned likelihood fit bounds the sidereal first-harmonic amplitude at 0.0086 (95% C.L., statistical). The analysis, frozen on the initial partial release, applied unchanged to the 229833 events of the later-released 1998 run confirms the null (amplitude 0.0018, p=0.90). Using the as-built SLC beam azimuth from the release's documentation corpus, we bound the asymmetry's anisotropy tensor in the Sun-centered frame: $ρ_1\le0.060$, $ρ_2\le0.18$, and, for vector backgrounds, $ρ_0\le0.092$ (95% C.L.). A leading-order matching maps these onto minimal Standard-Model-Extension coefficients as $10^{-2}$-level sensitivities to the two-time-index block of the electroweak gauge-sector coefficient $k_W$ (components with no existing laboratory constraint) and to the Higgs-sector coefficient $k_{ϕϕ}$; the insertions split the $Z$ pole by polarization, so for the tensor families assessed the resonance saturates the sidereal amplitude near $10^{-2}$ and the Born-model bounds exclude finite coefficient bands rather than set an upper limit. We also derive a previously unpublished $Z$-pole birefringence channel in the helicity-odd azimuthal modulation of the thrust axis, with response enhanced by about $2M_Z/Γ_Z$; a Born-level pilot is null. First sidereal analyses of hadronization and leptonic asymmetries bound instrumental drifts at the $10^{-4}$-$10^{-3}$ fractional level.

title: Latent Path Exploration via Potential-Guided Subtrajectory Balance
abstract: Continuous latent reasoning enables language models to perform intermediate computation without generating explicit reasoning traces. Advances in stochastic latent reasoning allow multiple paths to be sampled in continuous space, but stochasticity alone does not ensure effective exploration. A key challenge is guiding stochastic transitions between intermediate latent states toward useful reasoning paths. We introduce SubLAT, which couples a relative answer potential with Subtrajectory Balance to learn stochastic latent exploration. The relative potential evaluates the answer support of sampled states against replacement states, with a correctness signal at the terminal state. Subtrajectory Balance relates potential differences to forward and backward transition densities across subtrajectories of different lengths. The model is jointly trained with answer supervision, CoT supervision, and representation distillation. Experiments on arithmetic and deductive reasoning show increasing solution coverage with larger sampling budgets across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as improvements on several structural OOD benchmarks. Trajectory analyses reveal progressive divergence among sampled latent paths and higher mean relative potentials for correct trajectories across arithmetic benchmarks.

title: LoRe-MIM: Lost-or-Replaced Masked Image Modeling for Self-Supervised Representation Learning in Whole-Body PET/CT
abstract: Deep learning models for whole-body positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) hold significant clinical potential for disease detection, treatment planning, and response assessment. However, the time and cost associated with expert annotations remain major bottlenecks in developing robust and generalizable models. Although self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a promising approach to mitigating annotation scarcity, its application to whole-body PET/CT remains relatively underexplored due to the limited availability of large-scale datasets and the challenges associated with learning complementary cross-modal representations. To address these limitations, we curate a heterogeneous, multi-tracer, multi-institutional cohort comprising 6,531 whole-body PET/CT scans and propose LoRe-MIM (Lost-Or-Replaced Masked Image Modelling), a novel self-supervised framework designed to learn multimodal representations through masked image reconstruction. Specifically, LoRe-MIM introduces a masking strategy in which image regions are either replaced with zeros (Lost) or substituted with corresponding complementary imaging modality (Replaced), encouraging the model to capture both modality-specific characteristics and cross-modal relationships. We evaluate the learned representations across multiple downstream tasks, including multimodal PET/CT image reconstruction, patch-based classification into cancer vs. non-cancer, whole-body lesion segmentation, label-efficient training, and robustness assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that LoRe-MIM consistently outperforms the corresponding state-of-the-art baselines across these tasks, highlighting its potential as a scalable and generalizable self-supervised learning framework for whole-body PET/CT analysis.

title: MUSBRIC: LEGO-Compatible Pneumatic Muscle Bricks for Reconfigurable Musculoskeletal Robots
abstract: Musculoskeletal robots combine compliant actuators with articulated skeletons, but exploring alternative configurations often requires repeated fabrication. We present MUSBRIC, a modular hardware platform and accompanying MuJoCo-based simulator for reconfigurable musculoskeletal robots. LEGO-compatible endcaps turn fiber-reinforced extensile pneumatic artificial muscles into reusable, plug-and-play muscle bricks that connect directly to standard LEGO components. Experimentally identified actuator behavior supports corresponding musculoskeletal simulations. An elbow-joint prototype validates load-dependent flexion and extension, showing that pulley-guided routing enables reversible motion and a mechanical stop stabilizes the straight posture. A robotic hand demonstrates compliant grasping and multi-joint construction. Matched hardware and simulation sweeps across 15 leg configurations demonstrate systematic exploration of attachment geometry, while a quadruped assembled from four legs demonstrates walking. Together, these demonstrations span mechanism analysis, configuration exploration, and functional robot construction within a single reconfigurable system. The hardware designs and simulation code will be released as open source soon to facilitate reproduction and further development.

title: Gromov-Hausdorff versus Hausdorff distances for Euclidean submanifolds with positive reach
abstract: This paper is about comparing the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between a pair of sets to the Hausdorff distance between the pair. Recent work on this problem has focused on two settings, Riemannian manifolds and metric graphs. Here, we focus on embedded submanifolds of Euclidean space endowed with the Euclidean metric. We prove that when $\mathcal{M}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact connected embedded submanifold without boundary, with positive reach, and $\mathrm{A}\subset\mathcal{M}$ is a subset that is sufficiently dense in $\mathcal{M}$ with respect to the reach, the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is bounded below by $1/2$ of the Hausdorff distance between them. We extend this result in two ways. First, we show that the factor $1/2$ can be improved using Jung's theorem. Second, we prove bounds on the Gromov-Hausdorff distance for pairs of subsets of $\mathcal{M}$. When $\mathbb{S}^{1}$ is equipped with the two-dimensional Euclidean metric, the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between $\mathbb{S}^{1}$ and any sufficiently dense subset of $\mathbb{S}^{1}$ can be expressed explicitly as a function of the Hausdorff distance between the two. We use interleavings between geometric simplicial complexes, nerve lemmas, properties of reach and the nearest-point projection map, and the fundamental class to produce the inequalities for general $\mathcal{M}$. We use the Borsuk-Ulam theorem for $\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{S}^1\subset \mathbb{R}^2$.

title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

title: Levi-Civita's type theorem for projectively equivalent sub-Riemannian metrics on step 2 distributions
abstract: This paper extends the classical results of Eisenhart (1923) and Levi-Civita (1896) on the classification of pairs of germs of Riemannian metrics with the same geodesics, either as parametrized curves (affine equivalence) or as unparametrized curves (projective equivalence), to sub-Riemannian metrics on arbitrary step 2 distributions: at every stable point in the projective case and at every point in the affine case. This extends the results of Zelenko (2004) for contact and even-contact distributions and the affine result of Lin and Zelenko (2024) for step 2 distributions with ad-surjective Tanaka symbols; our projective result covers the ad-surjective case as well. In the affine case, we prove that if a sub-Riemannian metric admits an affinely equivalent metric that is not constantly proportional to it, then locally it is a product of two sub-Riemannian metrics. In the projective case, we prove the 2019 conjecture of Jean, Maslovskaya, and Zelenko on generalized Levi-Civita pairs; in particular, the distribution admits a product structure, the squares of its components are involutive, and the restrictions of the two metrics to each leaf of the corresponding foliation are conformal to each other under the appropriate pullback. The proof is based on a new graph-theoretic formalism, in which compatible moving frames are represented by the vertices and edges of certain graphs. As a byproduct, we introduce a new discrete invariant of step 2 nilpotent graded Lie algebras, the characteristic tuple. The compatible graphs are used on the open dense set where this tuple is locally constant; the resulting bracket relations are identities between smooth tensors, so they extend by continuity across the points where the tuple jumps. Consequently, our classification holds without any assumption of local constancy of the characteristic tuple.

title: Reversing Polarization through Tolerance-Aware Recommendation and Adaptive Diversification
abstract: Recommender systems face a tension between broadening exposure to diverse viewpoints and avoiding interactions that reinforce extreme positions. This tension is especially consequential in already polarized populations. Here we investigate whether recommendation strategies can reverse polarization rather than merely slow its development. Building on the Attraction--Repulsion Model of opinion dynamics, we introduce two complementary design principles: Tolerance-aware recommendation, which seeks to learn each individual's tolerance for disagreement and reduces exposure to viewpoints beyond that tolerance, and adaptive diversification, which broadens exposure for agents with more extreme opinions while retaining stronger personalization for moderates. Agent-based experiments show that highly personalized recommendations intensify polarization under polarized initial conditions. Tolerance awareness alone primarily slows polarization, whereas combining it with adaptive diversification can reduce polarization below its initial level and, under suitable conditions, restore consensus. Additional experiments incorporating persistent extreme influencers and a spiral-of-silence mechanism show that the combined strategy can mitigate polarization under social pressure and selective participation. To examine whether these findings extend beyond predefined opinion-update rules, we repeat the experiments on a simulated social platform populated by 100 LLM-driven agents prompted to move toward opinions similar to their own and away from those that differ substantially. Across three runs, the combined strategy is again the only recommendation policy tested that reverses polarization in every run. These findings distinguish polarization prevention from reversal and identify tolerance-aware, adaptive exposure as a promising recommendation design principle for reconnecting divided populations.

title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.

title: A complete solution to the reverse isoperimetric problem for $λ$-convex bodies
abstract: For a given $λ> 0$, a convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called $λ$-convex if it is the intersection of balls of radius $1/λ$. We show that among all $λ$-convex bodies in $\mathbb R^n$ of a given surface area, volume is minimized by the $λ$-convex lens, that is, the intersection of two balls of radius $1/λ$. This confirms a conjecture of Borisenko in all dimensions $n \geq 2$. Moreover, we extend this reverse isoperimetric inequality to all model spaces of constant curvature in arbitrary dimension and arbitrary $λ> 0$.

title: DolphinRouting: Cluster-Level Binary Routing for Disaggregated LLM Inference Serving
abstract: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with $k$-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.

title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

title: Drift-diffusion equations with saturation on $\mathbb{R}^d$
abstract: We study a class of nonlinear drift--diffusion equations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with saturation-type mobilities, not necessarily concave. Under structural assumptions on the mobility and potentials, bounded-domain approximations and local Caccioppoli estimates yield weak solutions for all positive times and an $L^1$-contraction estimate. The same estimates provide local space--time compactness of time translates, whose subsequential limits are weak solutions. Under additional confinement assumptions, uniform mass-tail estimates yield a mass-preserving, free-energy dissipating $C_0$-semigroup of $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$-contractions. In this confining setting, every trajectory converges strongly in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to a stationary state with the same mass, and the resulting time-limit operator is an $L^1$-contraction. Under the same assumptions, we also identify the unique global and $L^1$-local minimiser of the free energy at each fixed mass and prove that it is stationary under the semigroup.

title: Perturbations of Truncated Toeplitz operators
abstract: We investigate the structure of kernels of finite-rank perturbations of truncated Toeplitz operators. By realizing a perturbed truncated Toeplitz operator on a model space as a suitable matrix-valued truncated Toeplitz operator on an enlarged model space, we identify its kernel with a coordinate projection of the kernel of an associated block Toeplitz operator. This realization enables us to transfer the nearly $S^*$-invariant structure of Toeplitz kernels to the perturbed truncated setting. More precisely, for a perturbation of rank at most $n$, we show that the kernel of the perturbed truncated Toeplitz operator is nearly $S^*$-invariant with defect at most $2n+1$. We then extend the method to truncated Toeplitz operators on multiband spaces. In this setting, a perturbation of rank at most $n$ again preserves the finite-defect nearly $S^*$-invariant structure of the kernel, with the explicit upper bound $2n+2$ for the defect.

title: Large Magnetocaloric Effect and Adiabatic Temperature Change in the Tellurate: Gd2TeO6
abstract: We investigate the structural, magnetic, thermodynamic, and magnetocaloric properties of polycrystalline Gd2TeO6, a rare-earth tellurate unexplored for cryogenic magnetic refrigeration. Powder X-ray diffraction confirms single-phase orthorhombic symmetry (P212121), featuring two crystallographically distinct seven-coordinate Gd sites. Magnetization measurements reveal no conventional long-range magnetic ordering down to 2 K, although low-field magnetic irreversibility emerges below approximately 4 K. Curie-Weiss analysis yields a Weiss temperature of -1.25 K, indicating weak predominantly antiferromagnetic interactions. The magnetization reaches approximately 97% of the theoretical saturation moment at 7 T with negligible hysteresis. Heat-capacity measurements reveal no sharp zero-field anomaly above 2 K, while a broad field-induced maximum indicates redistribution of low-energy magnetic entropy. Debye-Einstein analysis separates the lattice and magnetic contributions. At 2.5 K, the maximum magnetic entropy changes (-DeltaSM) reach 21.40, 48.51, and 54.81 J kg-1 K-1 for field changes of 0-2, 0-5, and 0-7 T, respectively. The corresponding volumetric entropy change reaches 400.50 mJ cm-3 K-1. Measurements up to 14 T yield (-DeltaSM) = 63.51 J kg-1 K-1, approaching the theoretical limit of 64.25 J kg-1 K-1. The estimated adiabatic temperature change is approximately 22.7 K for 0-7 T. First-principles calculations with GGA+U approximation reveal competing antiferromagnetic states, highlighting Gd2TeO6 as a promising candidate for cryogenic magnetocaloric applications.

title: Topological Quantum Spin Liquids in a Ladder with Majorana fermions and p-wave Superconductivity
abstract: In this article, we address the possibility of topological quantum spin liquids with only short-range (spin) correlations in the whole phase diagram in a ladder system, through an exactly solvable model which represents a generalization of the two-dimensional Kitaev honeycomb spin model to a ribbon geometry. This system gives rise to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge fields emerging in a static way in the ground state through Majorana fermions which then produce either $0$ or $π$ flux. Through a quantum field theory perspective, mathematical and Density Matrix Renormalization Group results, we present our progress on the geometrical, topological and physical classification of this model through observables navigating on the whole phase diagram presenting three spin-liquid phases with a spin gap and a metallic phase in the sense of Majorana fermions. We propose a bulk-edge correspondence revealing the presence of protected zero-energy Majorana fermions at the edge in the phases with a gap and revealing also the presence of itinerant Majorana fermions in the bulk in the topological liquid phase. The proposed approach allows us to distinguish between properties of the brickwall ladder giving rise to a special line and those of the square ladder allowing for the gapless Majorana liquid phase. This model gives some hope on finding solutions for topological quantum spin models, e.g. with $π$ flux, on a square lattice geometry. This approach also allows for a correspondence onto models of topological superconductivity.

title: Structural signatures of primary and secondary relaxation during physical aging of a metallic glass
abstract: Physical aging drives glasses toward equilibrium and changes their thermodynamic and mechanical properties, but the accompanying microscopic structural evolution remains poorly understood. Here, using our recently developed low-background setup combining fast scanning calorimetry with \emph{in-situ} X-ray total scattering, we investigate microscopic structural changes during physical aging in Pd$_{42.5}$Cu$_{30}$Ni$_{7.5}$P$_{20}$ metallic glass. The measurements span an unprecedented six orders of magnitude in time and a temperature range extending from above the glass transition temperature to more than 150\,K below it. We observe dominant structural changes near the first and second peaks of the structure factor. Near and above the glass transition temperature, changes in the first sharp diffraction peak closely follow enthalpy relaxation and are associated predominantly with increasing degrees of medium-range ordering. At lower temperatures, the enthalpy evolution can no longer be described by this contribution alone, revealing an additional, faster relaxation process that correlates with changes near the second diffraction peak and thus short-range structural rearrangements, including increased Pd--Pd correlations. These results establish a direct connection between thermodynamic relaxation and structural evolution, providing strong evidence that primary and secondary aging processes are associated with distinct structural length scales.

title: Bulk gap stability and spectral flow for fermions with weak long-range interactions
abstract: We prove that weak long-range many-body interactions preserve the bulk gap of a free fermion system and that a quasi-local spectral flow transports the free ground state to ground states of the interacting system. Let $Φ_h$ be a free fermionic interaction, possibly including pairing terms, whose infinite-volume Majorana coefficient operator $h$ has no spectrum in $(-g,g)$, and let $\mathcal V$ be an even self-adjoint many-body interaction. For sufficiently small $|λ|$, we construct pure ground states $ω_λ$ of the interacting bulk system $Φ_λ=Φ_h+λ\mathcal V$ and quasi-local automorphisms $β_{0,λ}$ such that $ω_λ=ω_0\circβ_{0,λ}$, where $ω_0$ is the free ground state of $Φ_h$. Each $ω_λ$ has a GNS Hamiltonian with gap at least $g-C_*|λ| \|\mathcal V\|_*$, where $\|\cdot\|_*$ is the relevant interaction norm. Our result allows polynomial decay of both the free coefficients and the many-body interaction. For two-site interactions on a uniformly discrete point set $Γ\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, a sufficient condition is decay as $(1+|x-y|)^{-\varpi}$ with $\varpi>2d$, for both the hopping and pairing coefficients and the interaction terms. The spectral-flow generator preserves the spatial exponent of the polynomial interaction norm, and its automorphisms satisfy locality bounds at that exponent. If $h$ and $\mathcal V$ have stretched-exponential decay, so does the spectral-flow generator. The proof constructs the spectral flow and establishes the gap through an excitation-number comparison, using polynomial propagation bounds for evolved interactions proved in a companion paper.

title: Toward a Complete Interpretation of Global 21 cm Absorption Signals Using the Radio CMB
abstract: The global 21 cm signal is among the most direct probes of cosmic dawn, encoding information about when the first stars formed and how efficiently they heated their surroundings. However, such measurements are limited by bright Galactic foregrounds, ionospheric effects, and instrumental systematics. Even a confident detection would face a further obstacle: the brightness temperature depends on the spin temperature of the gas and the temperature of the radio background only through a single combination, so anomalous signals such as the EDGES (Bowman et al. 2018) absorption trough admit both cold gas and excess radio background interpretations. Recently, Holder et al. 2026 showed that resonant 21 cm absorption by high-redshift neutral hydrogen imprints an excess optical depth on CMB anisotropies at radio wavelengths, which depends on the spin temperature alone. Here we propose combining a measurement of the CMB hydrogen optical depth with the global signal to break this degeneracy, isolating the radio background temperature without the need for astrophysical modelling. Forecasting four interferometric configurations, we find that a compact $55 \times 55$ array of 6 m dishes observing for 4000 hours can establish an EDGES-like optical depth at $4.2σ$, while fiducial cosmic dawn histories require roughly an order of magnitude more collecting area. This constitutes a model-independent route to interpreting any global 21 cm detection.

title: Ricci curvature of semigroup walks on graphs and generator representations
abstract: We present an operator-theoretic framework for the Ollivier--Ricci curvature of (one-parameter families of) random walks generated by positive semigroups on graphs. On a metrically complete graph $(G,d)$ that is $d$-locally finite, we introduce a class of admissible semigroup random walks whose infinitesimal first-order approximation is itself a random walk. We prove that the Ollivier--Ricci curvature of an admissible semigroup random walk is well-defined and completely determined by its first-order approximation. We then establish a variational representation of the curvature of random walks in terms of a notion of the initial-time generator. This representation applies in particular to admissible semigroup random walks. Finally, we use this representation to define an operator-theoretic Ollivier--Ricci curvature for operators acting on spaces of functions over general metric spaces and establish sufficient conditions for well-definedness. This framework contains, in particular, Markovian random walks associated with discrete Laplacians.

title: Self-training for cross-centre coronary vessel segmentation in X-ray angiography using pre-contrast frame subtraction
abstract: Deep learning models for coronary vessel segmentation in X-ray angiography often perform poorly on data from centres that were not represented in training. Apart from differences in equipment, the labels of the largest public dataset (ARCADE) are incomplete, as only the segments defined in the SYNTAX score are annotated. In this study, we evaluated whether self-training with pseudo-labels can improve performance on external data without additional manual annotation. Pseudo-labels were generated from two sources, namely the predictions of an nnU-Net model trained on ARCADE and a contrast map obtained by subtracting a pre-contrast frame from the same sequence. The nnU-Net predictions were extended along the contrast map, and pixels detected only in the subtraction image were assigned an ignore label and excluded from the loss. Six models were trained and tested on ARCADE and on two external datasets (XCAD and XACV). All first-round models initialised with the baseline predictions performed better than both the baseline and a control model fine-tuned for the same number of epochs. The model trained on the XCAD pool improved the macro-averaged Dice score by 2.7 points (95% CI 2.3-3.2), while the control decreased it by 0.6 points. A second round of self-training did not lead to further improvement. When an external model trained on 50 fully annotated images was used to generate the initial labels, the XCAD Dice score increased from 0.623 to 0.745 without any XCAD labels, although performance on XACV did not improve because large main vessels were missed. These results suggest that the benefit of self-training depends largely on the sensitivity of the model used to generate the initial pseudo-labels.

title: Symmetric Structure and Motivic Transformation in Melodies, Phrases, and Themes
abstract: Transposition, inversion, and retrograde are fundamental operations in music theory, from Schoenberg's twelve-tone technique to Forte's set classes and Lewin's transformational theory, yet their use in melodies has rarely been quantified. We read a melodic line through the orbits and stabilizers of its windows of $m = 3-6$ notes under the group generated by these operations and cyclic shift. The window entropy splits into an orbit entropy (motivic vocabulary) and a within-orbit entropy normalized by orbit size (deployment), and the group elements relating windows of one orbit give the motivic transformations.
