A slice-consistent Brownian Bridge Diffusion Model was strengthened with multi-dataset training and data-source conditioning to enrich the anatomical prior learned from MRI, and with expanded multi-slice CT context to exploit the through-plane continuity of subject-specific anatomy in CT. Synthetic MRI was used for FreeSurfer-based anatomical parcellation and PET quantification, while deep-ensemble uncertainty was calibrated with conformal prediction to estimate a plausible range for the corresponding real MRI-based SUVR. On $^{11}$C-PiB PET from OASIS-3, the proposed method achieved the highest synthesis and parcellation fidelity among the compared methods. Mean cortical SUVR from the proposed synthetic MRI agreed closely with the real MRI-based reference (MAE $0.016 \pm 0.015$, Pearson $r = 0.9987$) and yielded the same amyloid-positivity classification as the real MRI in all 87 test subjects at the prespecified cut-off. Conformal prediction achieved empirical coverage close to the prespecified levels, and at 90% target coverage, 85 of 87 subjects had prediction intervals that supported an unambiguous amyloid-positivity decision. Zero-shot evaluation on an independent external cohort showed that the proposed CT-to-MRI model could support PET quantification without retraining, although conformal calibration required target-cohort recalibration to recover the intended coverage. These findings support CT-to-MRI-based MRI-free PET quantification as a promising approach for providing accurate SUVR measurements and an explicit assessment of their reliability.

title: Nonlinear Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons at van der Waals topological interfaces
abstract: Topological photonic structures provide a powerful means of confining and directing light through interface states formed between photonic phases with distinct topological properties. Van der Waals (vdW) materials offer complementary opportunities for nanophotonics: their optical properties can be selected from a wide family of layered crystals, while their atomically smooth surfaces and lack of lattice-matching constraints enable complex photonic heterostructures to be assembled layer by layer. This flexibility allows topological photonic confinement and strong excitonic coupling to be engineered separately within the same structure. Here, patterned low-loss dielectric hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) defines the photonic modes, while an encapsulated WSe2 monolayer provides the excitonic resonance that couples directly to the confined optical field. We use this approach to realise Jackiw-Rebbi exciton-polaritons in a one-dimensional hBN double-grating heterostructure. Strong coupling between the WSe2 exciton and a photonic Jackiw-Rebbi state localised at the interface between two topologically distinct gratings produces upper and lower Jackiw-Rebbi polariton branches. By varying the temperature from 4.7 to 300 K, we tune the exciton across the photonic bandgap and trace the evolution and anticrossing of these branches using angle-resolved reflectance and photoluminescence spectroscopy. Power-dependent photoluminescence further reveals a pronounced nonlinear response of the confined Jackiw-Rebbi polariton, including a blueshift of up to 5 meV and correlated changes in its intensity scaling and linewidth. These results establish vdW photonic heterostructures as a versatile platform for engineering tunable and nonlinear polaritons localised at topological interfaces.

title: AVPS-360: A Spatial Audio-Visual Benchmark for Instance Segmentation and Tracking of Sound-Producing Persons
abstract: Audio-visual instance segmentation (AVIS) segments and tracks individual sound-producing objects in videos. Existing benchmarks predominantly use monaural audio, which lacks inter-channel cues for spatially distinguishing concurrent sound sources. We introduce AVPS-360 (Audio-Visual Person Segmentation 360), a spatial audio-visual benchmark bridging AVIS and sound event localisation and detection (SELD). Built upon STARSS23, it pairs first-order Ambisonics audio with synchronised 360° video across 230 recordings totalling 10.5 hours. Recordings average 164.0 seconds. The dataset captures intermittent sound production in real-world interactions dominated by speech, alongside laughter, clapping, and footsteps. It provides 31,678 manually reviewed instance masks linked to source identities and sound-event labels. We also present a baseline that integrates spatial audio with visual features for frame-level segmentation and identity association across frames. Experiments on AVPS-360 show that existing AVIS methods struggle with detection and identity association in long recordings with intermittent sound production, while our baseline substantially improves performance in both aspects.

title: Lattice moments and quantum designs
abstract: We show that the ensemble of unimodular Gottesman$-$Kitaev$-$Preskill distributions fails to form a rigged quantum $3$-design and quantify the replica defect that determines this failure. This is established by rederiving a second moment formula for symplectic lattices in a self-contained manner.

title: FIRME: Registry-Anchored Memory Graphs for Evolving, Heterogeneous Investor Knowledge
abstract: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.

title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.

title: Cubic lower bounds for the permanent in odd characteristic, for Pfaffian representations, and for polynomial entries
abstract: The determinantal complexity of a polynomial is the order of the smallest matrix whose entries are polynomials of degree at most one and whose determinant equals the polynomial. A lower bound for the permanent in this measure is the algebraic form of the question whether the permanent is harder to compute than the determinant. Over the complex numbers, the best known lower bound grows cubically in the size of the permanent. It holds even when the permanent only has to be a limit of such determinants. I prove that the cubic lower bound holds over every algebraically closed field of odd characteristic $p$, with a constant that depends on $p$. Hence the cubic bound does not depend on characteristic zero. I also prove the bound for Pfaffians, which are square roots of determinants of skew symmetric matrices. Lower bounds for Pfaffians imply the same bounds for determinants. Further, I prove the bound, divided by $a$, for matrices whose entries are polynomials of degree at most $a$. All three results come from one lower bound for smooth hypersurfaces. I prove it in every characteristic by counting intersection points together with their multiplicities.

title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra
abstract: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-$D$ factor $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$, replacing isotropic Gaussian designs with power-law measurement covariance $Σ= \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$ leaves the Burer--Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalised first-order optimizers stall above a critical exponent $s^\ast$. We trace this failure to a numerical precision wall. At the ground truth, the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales at leading order as $V^{-(s+1)}D^{-s}$. When this curvature drops below the effective denominator floor $ε_O$ of optimizer $O$, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, yielding the leading-order boundary $s^\ast_O(V, D) = [\log(1/ε_O) - \log V]/\log(VD) + δ_O$, where $δ_O$ is a metric-dependent detection lag. With $δ_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ calibrated on four configurations and frozen, this formula predicts Adam's onset within $0.45$ across all 16 cells of a held-out grid ($V \in \{64,128,256,512\} \times D \in \{4,8,16,32\}$), separates fixed-$VD$ pairs, and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at $D = 2$, reflects a finite-$D$ spectral crossover, and saturates below $\varepsilon_0 = 10^{-8}$ at a dynamical floor.

title: Average pairwise Hamming distance of a subset in a hypercube
abstract: In this note, we prove that for a subset $\mathcal{F}$ of $\{0,1\}^n$ of density $\frac{1}{8}$, its average pairwise Hamming distance is at least $\frac{n-3}{2}$, with equality attained only by $(n-3)$-dimensional subcubes. This answers a question of Lei Yu, and solves an important open case of a more general question posed by Ahlswede and Katona in 1977.

title: MetaRefine: Score Refinement with Multi-Level Features for Image Assessment
abstract: An image's original dimensions, aspect ratio, and composition provide important cues that can affect its technical and aesthetic quality. Image assessment methods use resizing, cropping, padding, or patch sampling to accommodate different input sizes. However, these operations can alter or obscure original geometric and compositional cues. Existing assessment models also encode rich multi-level visual evidence that can be further extracted and exploited to improve existing models. This motivates us to combine visual evidence with original-image geometry for score refinement without changing the original scoring pipelines. In this paper, we introduce MetaRefine, a metadata-aware score refinement architecture whose lightweight residual heads predict score corrections from geometry, multi-level visual features, and the frozen model's original score. Across 100 configurations on 21 datasets, MetaRefine improves PLCC in 88 configurations and SRCC in 85, with average relative gains of 7.55% and 7.10%, respectively. It reduces MAE in 90 configurations and RMSE in 89, with average relative reductions of 23.27% and 21.93%, respectively. The median parameter overhead is only 1.11%. MetaRefine can further improve state-of-the-art (SOTA) assessment models on multiple benchmarks.

title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
abstract: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

title: Multiple representations in difference sets under polynomial density constraints
abstract: Motivated by the classical study of additive representation functions and the combinatorial phenomenon of sum-difference asymmetry, we investigate the subtractive representation function $d_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}(n)$, which counts the number of solutions of the equation $n = b - a$ with $a\in \mathcal{A}$ and $b\in \mathcal{B}$. Specifically, we study lower bounds and the asymptotic behavior of $d_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}(n)$ under polynomial density constraints of orders $x^α$ and $x^{1-α}$, where $0 < α< 1$. We first establish a general lower bound for the first moment of $d_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}(n)$. Furthermore, by employing a recursive construction, we prove that this lower bound is essentially optimal under certain regularity assumptions on the counting functions. Finally, utilizing probabilistic methods, we show the existence of sets for which $d_{\mathcal{B},\mathcal{A}}(n)$ has a logarithmic point-wise upper bound.

title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

title: Weak Factor Recovery in Sparse Bayesian Factor Models under Exchangeable Shrinkage Process Prior
abstract: Sparse Bayesian factor models provide a flexible framework for learning low-dimensional latent structure in multivariate data, but inference on the number of active factors remains challenging when some factors are weak or highly sparse. We study weak factor recovery under a variance based exchangeable shrinkage process (ESP) prior. We derive the posterior factor activation mechanism and show that, conditional on the global and local shrinkage parameters, activation is governed by the standardised loading energy together with the ESP prior activation odds. This yields an explicit activation boundary and clarifies how signal strength, sparsity, the number of observed variables, and the truncation level affect recovery. Simulation experiments show a clear transition between shrinkage and recovery around this boundary and demonstrate that sparsity can substantially affect activation even when raw loading energy is held fixed. They further show that factor activation and recovery of the relative loading pattern across variables can behave differently. These results clarify when weak latent factors become difficult to distinguish from redundant components under ESP shrinkage.

title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
abstract: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{https://github.com/AgenticOrgLab/AgenticUniversity.git}.

title: SPECTRUM: A Strategic Framework and Technical Blueprint for European Exascale Research Data and Compute Infrastructure
abstract: The HiLumi LHC, the SKA Observatory and LOFAR 2.0 will take High Energy Physics (HEP) and Radio Astronomy (RA) towards exabyte-scale data within the next decade, beyond the capacity of today's infrastructure. The SPECTRUM project responded with two documents built on the same evidence. A Technical Blueprint describes a European compute and data continuum as a capability map, consolidates the gaps found in HEP, RA and related use cases, and recommends technical actions in eight areas. A Strategic Research, Innovation and Deployment Agenda (SRIDA) organises thirteen priorities in four pillars, maps them to investment areas and European funding instruments, and phases them over a roadmap set against the timelines of the three instruments. This paper, by editors and contributors of both documents, summarises them, their consultative method and the impact the SRIDA expects.

title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
abstract: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

title: LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation
abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

title: Real-rooted Ehrhart $h^*$-polynomials of crown posets and wheel and whirl matroids
abstract: We prove that the Ehrhart $h^*$-polynomials of crown order polytopes are real-rooted, settling a conjecture of Lundström and Saud Maia Leite. For each integer $r\ge3$, the crown order polytope on $2r$ elements and the rank-$r$ whirl base polytope have the same $h^*$-polynomial. The $h^*$-polynomials of the rank-$r$ wheel and whirl base polytopes, as well as every convex combination of the two, have $2r-2$ distinct negative roots. Their coefficient sequences are positive, unimodal, and strictly ultra log-concave of order $2r-2$.

title: A Parameterized Stochastic Hamiltonian Process on Graphs with Two-Point Boundary Conditions
abstract: This paper presents a Lagrangian framework to solve Wasserstein Hamiltonian flows (WHF) under two-point boundary conditions on large finite graphs. Characterized by a coupled system of discrete master equation and Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) equation on the probability simplex, this formulation defines the macroscopic WHF. While classical density-based solvers can track this flow, they face severe memory and computational bottlenecks as the graph scale grows. To bypass these limitations, we introduce the stochastic Hamiltonian process (SHP), a sample-based mathematical framework that tracks individual particle dynamics rather than the full node-wise density. We parameterize the time-dependent potential using neural network, yielding the Neural SHP solver. Numerical experiments on synthetic graphs demonstrate the scalability of our method relative to density-based baselines. Furthermore, we validate Neural SHP across two large-scale real-world networks, a PubMed citation network and a massive road network, demonstrating its robust efficiency for graph partition and routing problems on complex graph structures.

title: Dihedral pointed fusion categories: diagrammatics, 3-cocycle representatives, and planar algebras
abstract: We construct a diagrammatic presentation by generators and relations for all dihedral pointed fusion categories $\mathrm{Vec}_{\mathrm{D}_{2n}}^ω$. Applying a jellyfish algorithm on our diagrammatics, we obtain an explicit closed formula for a complete set of normalized 3-cocycle representatives of $\mathrm{D}_{2n}$. As applications of our diagrammatics, we prove a universal property and show that in some cases we can recover affine $A$ unshaded subfactor planar algebras. We then extend our presentation to obtain diagrammatics for all pivotal structures on $\mathrm{Vec}_{\mathrm{D}_{2n}}^ω$.

title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
abstract: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

title: On the existence of minimizers for the generalized liquid drop model
abstract: We consider a broad class of generalized liquid drop models in which a perimeter term competes with repulsive nonlocal interactions with finite first moments. For all such kernels satisfying the natural physical assumption of reflection positivity we show existence of minimizers for all masses, in the (super-)critical regime. Moreover, in the subcritical regime we give the first quantitative estimate of the range of masses for which existence holds, which converges to the whole positive real line as one approaches the critical regime. This result builds on the nonlocal curvature approach introduced and developed in the periodic setting in \cite{dr24}.

title: Curvature Blindness: Material Inference in Stars and Black Hole Candidates
abstract: Gravitational observations can leave material properties undetermined in two different ways: distinct states can have the same total source, and distinct spacetime histories can have the same retained observations. We organize these inverse problems in general relativity through a property-level identifiability criterion, with applications to stars and black hole candidates. Two ideal massless gases illustrate equal-source ambiguity: their temperatures differ by a factor of $(8/29)^{1/4}$ and their entropies differ while their stress-energy tensors agree. A separate causal-fluid example starts with identical sources and geometric data but different constitutive responses; the two models' curvature histories separate at linear order in proper time and their scale factors at cubic order. For black hole candidates, the relevant distinction is between stationary exterior parameters, perturbing fluxes and constituent history. The framework provides a test for whether retained data identify a material property, separating instantaneous source equality, history-wide source equality and observational projection.

title: A Two-Wheeled Quadrotor with All-Clockwise Tilted Rotors for Level-Attitude Surface Locomotnion
abstract: Conventional wheel-equipped quadrotor UAVs must tilt their bodies to generate lateral forces, limiting their ability to maintain a desired attitude during lateral motion. This paper proposes a wheeled quadrotor with all-clockwise tilted rotors that uses surface contact as a constraint to generate propulsion along the contact surface without tilting the vehicle. We analyze feasible forces and system controllability under surface contact and optimize the vehicle design considering different rotor-spin configurations. The optimization results show that a configuration in which all four rotors spin clockwise can generate a larger tangential force than the conventional alternating-spin configuration. This approach enables both aerial and contact-based locomotion without additional rotor-tilting actuators or mechanisms. Simulation results demonstrate both hovering in free space and horizontal locomotion on a floor while maintaining a level attitude.

title: Algebraic World Model: From Exploration to Proofs
abstract: AI has made remarkable progress in mathematics, solving challenging problems with machine-checkable proofs in Lean, yet typically relying on predefined mathematical definitions and formal specifications. This raises a natural question: can it reason rigorously about an unknown world? We introduce the Algebraic World Model (AWM), a framework that turns interaction with unfamiliar environments into explicit mathematical models supporting formal reasoning. AWM explores the environment and develops executable Python hypotheses, continually testing and revising them against observations. It then structures these hypotheses into typed objects and shared rules, simplifies their structure through category-theory-guided transformations, and formalizes the resulting model in Lean 4 to prove reachability and impossibility. AWM can formally prove that a goal is unreachable, even beyond explored trajectories. On two impossible game levels, it constructs closed, kernel-checked Lean proofs excluding every legal winning sequence in all six runs, while Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, equipped with coding tools, produce none in twelve baseline runs. Four of AWM's six initial bounds are correct, compared with one for Opus 5.5 and none for GPT-6 Astra; given only feedback that a cheaper win exists, AWM revises its rules and constructs new proofs, reaching six of six correct bounds. Moreover, AWM produces interpretable mathematical models whose rules can be inspected and tested step by step. Across all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, these models enable Lean to replay the winning trajectories of all 183 levels and generalize beyond observed play, predicting unseen transitions and detecting changes in game mechanics. With Claude Opus 5, AWM clears all levels with a score of 99.9, while its certified winning trajectories use only 43% of the human baseline's actions.

title: Using domain walls to benchmark fast quantum anneals
abstract: We consider the distribution of domain walls arising in ground states of frustrated 1-dimensional Ising spin chains with anti-parallel boundary spins. For ideal chains, a sine-squared particle-in-a-box distribution of domain walls is expected in the quantum setting, and a uniform distribution expected classically. However, for chains with random imperfections, prior work [Chancellor et al., npj Quantum Inf. 8, 73, 2022] found that the distribution in a physical implementation corresponded to neither. Instead, the domain wall distribution forms a U-shaped profile arising from a classical model with random fields, where the combination of averaging over these fields and thermal averaging produces the characteristic U-shape. With D-Wave's newer fast anneal feature, we access anneal times shorter than the coherence time and observe the expected coherent quantum behavior in the form of a sine-squared distribution. For the shortest available anneal time, the dynamics have not yet reached the sine-squared shape and instead display a different U-shape in the middle of the chains. This motivates using the extent of the domain wall distribution tail in this regime as a platform independent metric that provides a signature of both coherence time and noise levels.

title: Discovering Interpretable Acoustic Features in Autoregressive Voice-Cloning TTS Models
abstract: Voice-cloning TTS models synthesize an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts, but it remains unclear which acoustic properties they represent and use. We introduce a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, analyzing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions via sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability. We focus on Qwen3-TTS and extend probing and steering to $5$ additional models to test generalization across architectures. These models encode concepts like pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering are effective only for some concepts. Strong probing does not always translate to steering or vice-versa. SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds $684$ automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond known concepts. Overall, we perform a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models.

title: High-throughput quantification of interfacial protein load in monodisperse oil-in-water emulsions
abstract: Food proteins play a critical role as emulsifiers, where adsorption at the oil and water interface governs emulsion formation and stability. However, quantitative characterization of interfacial protein load remains challenging due to polydispersity in conventional emulsification methods. We combine microfluidic generation of monodisperse emulsions with colorimetric protein quantification to measure the post-collection initial interfacial load ($Γ_0$) and subsequently monitored over 48 h to obtain the saturation load ($Γ_\infty$). Interfacial load exhibited a strong bulk concentration-dependent trend and was well described by a pseudo-first-order model. Both $Γ_0$ and $Γ_\infty$ followed sublinear scaling with concentration ($Γ_0$ ~ C^{0.21}$, $Γ_\infty$ ~ C^{0.12}$). Interfacial loads were largely independent of droplet diameter, with modest reductions in initial loading for the smallest droplets at low protein concentration. Measured loads exceeded idealized monolayer predictions and fell between bilayer and trilayer bounds, consistent with accumulation beyond a simplified monolayer model. Additionally, high-throughput mapping was performed across three proteins, seven concentrations, three pH values, and two ionic strengths, revealing that $α$-Casein exhibited higher interfacial loads than $β$-Casein and Whey protein Isolate, with maximum adsorption near the isoelectric point and at elevated ionic strength. In summary, this study establishes a quantitative experimental framework for linking protein properties, formulation conditions, and interfacial behavior using monodisperse microfluidic emulsions, while requiring only milligram-scale protein quantities.

title: RecHash: Segmented Hash-Entangled Chains for Stateful Sequential Authentication
abstract: RecHash is a stateful sequential authentication construction based on paired hash-chain openings and an authenticated record history. It develops the decreasing position relation of the 2019 hash-entangled construction, whose exact integer normalization yields a two-coordinate constant-sum antichain. Direct proportional reuse is constrained by integer capacity and multiplicative contraction. The main construction instead assigns each record to a predetermined chain segment, with complementary positions encoding each digest block. All digests fit every scheduled slot, independently of preceding messages. For an $\ell$-bit digest distributed over $k$ equal-length chain pairs, balanced allocation gives $\lfloor L/(2^{\lceil\ell/k\rceil}+1)\rfloor$ slots. A 256-bit digest, 32 pairs, and length 65535 provide 254 application records followed by a renewal certificate, with 2048 bytes of openings per record for 256-bit chain outputs. We give a complete segmented state transition, a worked trace, exact allocation and resource results, and a renewal-free security-composition theorem conditional on authenticated history and an adaptive one-step guarantee. The analysis relates the construction to constant-sum encodings and standardized hash-based signatures; a concrete post-quantum reduction and security across renewal remain open.

title: Differentiation and Shift Property Characterisations of the Group Fourier Transform on the Heisenberg Group
abstract: Recently, Krukowski characterised the classical Fourier transform on the real line in terms of its behaviour with respect to differentiation. For locally compact abelian groups, he obtained a characterisation based on the behaviour of the Fourier transform under the shift. Each of these results assumed that the operator (to be characterised) is an integral transform (with a kernel satisfying suitable regularity conditions), paired with a normalisation which he refers to as the Dirac delta property. In this paper, we obtain analogous results for the group Fourier transform on the Heisenberg group. Here, the differentiation property is formulated in terms of the behaviour of the group Fourier transform with respect to the left-invariant vector fields, and the shift property is based on its behaviour under right translation. Both of these characterise the group Fourier transform on the Heisenberg group, once paired with a Dirac delta property. Our results assume that the transform is continuous and linear, and do not require it to be an integral transform a priori.

title: Random Matching Between Distinct Distributions in Two Dimensions
abstract: Given two independent $n$-point samples drawn from possibly distinct probability distributions on a compact 2-dimensional surface, we minimize the total squared distance over all perfect bipartite matchings. Under regularity assumptions, the expected matching cost minus $n$ times the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the sampling distributions grows logarithmically with $n$. We determine this difference up to an additive $o(1)$ error, including the dependence of the logarithmic coefficient and constant term on geometry and sampling distributions, and establish the existence of a universal constant shared by these formulas. Our analysis expresses the expected matching cost in terms of the cost of transporting a heat-smoothed sample back to its original points. The reductions giving this relation hold in every dimension and for general costs under suitable assumptions, with consequences beyond the setting studied here. In two dimensions, the relation is exact up to an additive $o(1)$ error, so determining the matching cost amounts to evaluating the smoothing cost with the same accuracy. We obtain this evaluation by subdividing the domain and exploiting cancellations between the sample and its own smoothing.

title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
abstract: We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $β=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$α< α_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings. Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms. To establish our results, we first develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, which resolves short-cycle fluctuations in the complex plane by lifting classical small subgraph conditioning on random regular graphs to random holomorphic functions. Second, we overcome the standard second-moment barrier caused by the exponential blowup of the bare second moment inside the replica-symmetric phase, by showing that replica symmetry implies a nonpositive Bethe functional and upgrading planted overlap concentration to an exponentially small bound, which enables a typical-graph truncation that controls complex second moments up to the replica symmetry breaking threshold.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

title: An SCL-Aware Design of PAC Codes
abstract: We develop design methodologies for the rate profile of polarization-adjusted convolutional (PAC) codes tailored to successive cancellation list (SCL) decoding. The crux of our approach is two-fold: first is the creation of a modified density evolution Gaussian approximation (DEGA), called conditional DEGA (CDEGA), to analyze the decoding process in the presence of errors; second is the creation of a dangerous-path occupancy metric to find the conditional occupancy of bit-errors in a finite list. Our approach not only illuminates the role of rate-one precoding, but also provides insight into why certain information sets are particularly well suited to PAC codes. We demonstrate the usefulness of CDEGA and dangerous-path metrics with algorithms that create new information sets, as well as precoders that are extremely sparse yet competitive. In particular, we design codes of length $N \leq 512$ with various rates and list sizes, all of which offer at least half a dB gain over traditional PAC codes at an FER of $10^{-3}$ and improve upon state-of-the-art results.

title: A case study of hybrid statistical models for analyzing spatio-temporal effects in historical map series of Donau-Ries county
abstract: This case study compares generalized linear models, generalized additive models, and semi-structured deep distributional regression for analyzing settlement patterns in historical land-cover maps. Using four reference years for Donau-Ries county (Landkreis Donau-Ries) in southern Germany, we quantify how distances to agricultural areas, forests, and rivers relate to residential presence, and we evaluate predictive performance through spatial block cross-validation. Classical models yield stable and interpretable distance effects, whereas the semi-structured framework improves prediction once local image context is included. The analysis illustrates a practical trade-off between interpretability, accuracy, and robustness when interpretable covariates are combined with deep components in spatio-temporal data analysis.

title: Localization in Seven-Dimensional Supergravity
abstract: Seven-dimensional supergravity provides holographic access to strongly coupled six-dimensional superconformal theories through its highest-dimensional supersymmetric AdS vacua. Its unique spinor-bilinear geometry and massive higher-form dynamics make systematic analysis and solution-finding distinctively challenging. Relative equivariant localization can obtain supersymmetric observables in odd dimensions from fixed-point data on an auxiliary even-dimensional filling, without an explicit solution. We extend this approach to seven dimensions in maximal Cartan-gauged supergravity with all gauge fields active. We formulate the Euclidean action and Killing-spinor equations in terms of field strengths, and construct a bilinear system adapted to the change in spinor reality conditions from symplectic-Majorana to Majorana. On the non-null gauged active spinor branch, independent, oppositely R-charged spinors are paired by Majorana conjugation on the same complex background. One algebraic gauging correction and two algebraic bilinear projections suffice to extend the equal-charge sector to independent Cartan charges, and the underlying efficient reorganization also applies in the Lorentzian theory. Massive 3-form self-duality fixes the quartic anomaly class and determines the higher-form fixed-point datum from Abelian moment maps. Localization at the single fixed point of the filling recovers the general supersymmetric AdS$_7$ black-hole action, without extending the solution. We prove gauge-covariant Killing-spinor invariance under the combined supersymmetric Killing flow and R-symmetry action, deriving the linear chemical-potential constraint. Extremizing the constrained entropy functional and requiring real positive stationary entropy yields the nonlinear charge relation within the Euclidean analysis, equivalent to Lorentzian horizon extremality for the known spherical black-hole family.

title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
abstract: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

title: Global Well-Posedness of Landau Equation in Bounded Domains
abstract: We prove global well-posedness of the Landau equation near a Maxwellian in bounded $C^3$ domains with in-flow or diffuse-reflection boundary conditions for $-3\leqγ\leq1$, including Coulomb interactions. Small compatible Gaussian perturbations generate global strong solutions, with uniqueness and continuous dependence among weak solutions. The proof combines energy estimates, the comparison principle, interior and weighted boundary estimates for velocity derivatives up to second order, and a logarithmic estimate for solution difference.

title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws
abstract: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.

title: Petersson-rigid lattices of signature (2,1) and their harmonic weak Maass forms
abstract: An even lattice $L$ of signature $(2,1)$ is Petersson-rigid if the orthogonal group of its discriminant form acts absolutely irreducibly on the space of cusp forms of weight $\frac32$ for its Weil representation, a space of dimension at least two. We prove, with computer assistance, that there are exactly twelve such lattices up to isometry, and we determine their root bases. Four of them are theta lattices, whose cusp forms are lifts of unary theta series. On each, the space is $\mathbb C F_0\otimesσ_0$ for one form $F_0$ and an irreducible $σ_0$, so the Petersson norm is $\|F\|^2=t_μ\|c_F(μ)\|^2$ for all cusp forms $F$, with one $t_μ>0$, $μ$ the least exponent of $F_0$ and $c_F(μ)$ the coefficient of $q^μ$ in $F$. We prove that the harmonic weak Maass forms of weight $\frac12$ in the $σ_0$-isotypic part with a pole of least possible order are exactly the forms $\mathcal H_F$ with principal part $q^{-μ}\overline{c_F(μ)}$, and $ξ_{1/2}\mathcal H_F=F/t_μ$. For the four theta lattices it is a theorem that $t_μ=\frac{s-1}{12}\sqrt s$, with $s$ the square-free part of $|\det L|/2$, and the $\mathcal H_F$ come from umbral moonshine. For the eight others we compute $F_0$, $t_μ$ and $\mathcal H_{F_0}$: the Hecke eigenvalues are integers and, at the primes computed, the $a_p$ of an elliptic curve, and for three of the eight $F_0$ is explicit as an eta-theta product. We prove, for every prime $p>3$, a closed formula in $p$ and one class number for the difference $g(X_0(4p)/w_p)-g(X_0(2p)/w_p)$ of the genera of two Atkin-Lehner quotients of modular curves. In a family $\mathcal D_p$ of discriminant forms, $p$ an odd prime, containing three of the eight, comparison with that classification shows that $\mathcal D_p$ is rigid exactly when $X_0(4p)/w_p$ has genus $1$ and $X_0(2p)/w_p$ has genus $0$.

title: Quantitative sub-ballisticity of self-avoiding walk on $\mathbb{Z}^d$
abstract: We prove quantitative sub-ballisticity for the self-avoiding walk on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $d\geq 2$. Namely, we obtain an explicit exponential rate of decay for the probability that a self-avoiding walk of length $n$ reaches distance at least $vn$, in terms of $v>0$. As a consequence, we show that the displacement of an $n$-step self-avoiding walk is at most $n/\exp(c\log^* n)$ with very high probability. Previously, only a non-quantitative $o(n)$ bound was known from the work of Duminil-Copin and Hammond. Along the way, we show that at criticality the partition function of bridges of length $n$ is on average bounded by $C/\log\log n$, which we believe to be of independent interest. Our approach is based on a quantitative analysis of the original nonconstructive proof of Duminil-Copin and Hammond using ideas from proof theory.

title: Directed Cut-Query Complexity of Finding a King
abstract: A king in a tournament is a vertex from which every other vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two. We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a king when a query specifies a set of vertices and returns the number of edges directed from that set to its complement. We prove that this complexity is $Θ(n)$ for $n$-vertex tournaments. To show this, we first show that every correct deterministic algorithm in this model must output a maximum-outdegree vertex, even though a king need not have maximum outdegree. We then give an adversary whose answers, after too few queries, remain consistent with a tournament in which the algorithm's output does not have maximum outdegree.

title: Dynamic Powergrid Optimization with FPGA-based Neuromorphic Higher-order Ising Machines
abstract: The advent of large, high-density FPGAs such as the AMD Versal enables efficient hardware implementation of neuromorphic Ising machines, unlocking unprecedented performance for complex combinatorial optimizations. A critical application for this computing paradigm is dynamic powergrid optimization, specifically Distribution Network Reconfiguration (DNR), which seeks to mitigate severe resistive losses and reduce electricity costs by optimizing network switch configurations in real time. This paper presents an FPGA-based neuromorphic higher-order Ising machine for high-speed, adaptive DNR. By directly mapping DNR onto higher-order Ising interactions via a polynomial unconstrained binary optimization (PUBO) formulation, the proposed architecture requires only 179 spins for the IEEE 33-bus network, which represents a 6 times reduction compared to standard quadratic formulations. Implemented on an AMD Versal Premium VP1802 FPGA, the architecture executes parallel spin-group updates every 20 ns and solves 33-, 51-, and 69-bus benchmark networks with median latencies of 1.6-29.3 ms, yielding a 7-58 times speedup over Gurobi to the first optimal solution. Using the solver with expanded network-switching flexibility reduces power loss by 80.71 kW (57.83%), while adaptive reconfiguration every 10 s under time-varying demand saves 131.16 kWh/day over static daily reconfiguration, highlighting the potential of higher-order Ising hardware for fast, adaptive smart grid management.

title: On the gauge-invariant orbital angular momentum of vector optical vortices in the paraxial approximation and beyond
abstract: In this paper we present a gauge-invariant formalism for describing the spin and orbital angular momenta of scalar and vector optical vortices. The correction term, arising from consistent incorporation of the transverse vector potential's nonlocality, restores gauge invariance and makes it possible to separate the total angular momentum into spin and orbital components. We propose a method for calculating the orbital and spin angular momenta of multimode vector vortex fields and show that the orbital angular momentum of such beams contains two qualitatively different components. The polarization-independent contribution to the orbital angular momentum is related to the topological charge that determines the order of the phase singularity, while the polarization-dependent one is proportional to the helical topological charge that determines the spatial inhomogeneity of the polarization. We also discuss the quantization procedure for fields with spatially inhomogeneous polarization in terms of modes with a helical topological charge, and examine the limits of applicability of the proposed formalism.

title: A heterogenetic theory of living systems
abstract: The problem of the dynamics of living systems and their mathematical representation essentially unfolds on two levels. Firstly, the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure describe how a living system produces and maintains itself. Secondly, living phenomena are recognised as historical, involving the evolution of dynamics and spaces of possibility that change over time. Currently, no differential model can incorporate both of these aspects. We propose adopting the differential heterogenesis framework, which enables us to define differential operators that change in space and time, producing event-based and historical dynamics. In this construction, heterogeneous operator assemblages will be constrained by the principles of autopoiesis and operational closure, providing a theoretical framework for event-based and historical living systems. Finally, we provide a specific example of assembly with Gray-Scott kinetic equations, along with numerical simulations and results.

title: CrossWeave: Cross-Modal Scene and Instance Retrieval from Sparse 2D-3D Alignment
abstract: Cross-modal scene and instance retrieval aims to retrieve a corresponding 3D environment or object given query 2D images, serving as a foundational mechanism for spatial reasoning in robotics and AR/VR. Existing methods achieve this by learning alignment only at the level of whole scenes or objects, which provides no supervision for the fine-grained local structure within them. In this work, we show that supervision on a set of sparse 2D-3D correspondences, without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives, is sufficient to train a single model for both scene- and instance-level retrieval. Specifically, we propose $\textbf{CrossWeave}$, a novel framework for cross-modal retrieval that learns sparse patch-point alignment, which alone outperforms existing methods. An optimal transport-based aggregator over the aligned features gives further gains by clustering structurally redundant regions, freeing descriptor capacity for semantically distinct local features. CrossWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance on both scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan with a $\textit{single model}$, whereas existing methods require separate models for each task. Our results suggest that whole-scene encoding is unnecessary for cross-modal retrieval and that sparse local correspondence supervision is a more effective and flexible alternative.

title: Quasi-Phases of Quantum Matter
abstract: Within quantum many-body phase diagrams, continuous transition lines can appear and then terminate. However, it has remained unclear whether the neighboring regimes can be meaningfully described as distinct phases, akin to water and vapour, since any sharp characterization would have to go beyond the usual notion of phases of matter. We answer this in the affirmative by introducing quasi-phases: gapped regimes near a critical point that are connected in the broader phase diagram, but not by any gapped path accessible from small perturbations of the critical theory. The physical consequences include interface modes between regimes in the same phase of matter. More striking still, describing both the extended critical line and the gapped path connecting the regimes requires a bigger multicritical parent theory. In spin-chain examples with continuous terminating lines with central charge $c=1$, we find multicritical $c=3/2$ and $c=9/5$ orbifolds describing so-called 'quotient symmetry protected' and 'representation symmetry protected' topological phenomena. While one-dimensional symmetry-protected topological phases are labeled by projective representation classes, these quasi-phases can have interface modes carrying higher-dimensional linear representations. We turn this into a constructive principle through a weakening of the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis anomaly. Supporting distinct quasi-phases makes an unnecessary critical point infrared-necessary, even if it is unnecessary at the ultraviolet scale. This condition is more restrictive than simply having a codimension-one critical line, revealing richer structure within phases of matter than their conventional classification suggests.

title: Mapping Stellar Obliquity Across Space and Time
abstract: The angle between a star's rotational angular momentum vector and the orbital angular momentum vector of its planets---stellar obliquity---encodes the initial conditions and dynamical history of planetary systems. Variations in obliquity with orbital separation may arise from either primordial disk structure (e.g., broken or warped protoplanetary disks with misaligned inner and outer regions) or subsequent dynamical interactions with planets or external perturbers. Comparing obliquities across orbital distance therefore probes the spatial imprint of these processes, while comparisons across age constrain their temporal evolution. To test for signatures of obliquity evolution in both space and time, we compare stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single Sun-like stars spanning four samples that probe distinct regimes of orbital separation and age: 49 protoplanetary disk systems, 24 debris disk systems, 21 warm Jupiter systems, and 20 hot Jupiter systems. We find minimum misalignment rates of $33^{+7}_{-6}$% for protoplanetary disk systems, $21^{+9}_{-7}$% for debris disk systems, $23^{+10}_{-8}$% for warm Jupiter systems, and $20^{+9}_{-8}$% for hot Jupiter systems. These rates are consistent within 1$σ$ across all samples. The absence of significant variation in minimum-obliquity distributions with either orbital separation or system age suggests that stellar obliquities for Sun-like stars may be largely established at formation with limited subsequent evolution in both space and time. These results are consistent with post-formation inclination evolution being either infrequent, confined to small misalignments, or restricted to regions of parameter space not examined here---such as systems with close stellar companions, hot host stars, small planets, and long-period giant planets.

title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
abstract: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

title: Thermodynamics of Swirling Black Holes and Kerr-Taub-NUT
abstract: We establish the first law of black hole thermodynamics for the recently discovered Kerr swirling (KS) and accelerated Kerr swirling (AKS) black hole solutions. We also revisit the first law for the Kerr-Taub-NUT (KTN) spacetime. Guided by Noether's original insight that global symmetries give rise to conservation laws, we employ and adapt the surface charge method for computing the associated charges (mass and angular momentum) in the presence of spacetime string-like defects (conical singularities) along the axes of both KS and KTN black holes. We obtain finite integrated charges in a quasi-local manner, without relying on the non-flat asymptotic regions characteristic of these spacetimes. We then establish a first law without introducing independent stringy terms unrelated to symmetries. For both KS and KTN, the quantities that play the role of the black hole entropy differ from the simple geometrical rule of one-fourth of the horizon area. This mismatch arises because we keep first-law charges associated with conservation laws. It indicates that standard formulas may not be naively used for black holes with string-like defects; they have a different topology and suggest the need for a new geometrical framework. In stark contrast, for the AKS spacetime, which can be regularized outside the singularity and lacks string-like defects, we find that the charges are consistent with a first law having the usual one-fourth of the area entropy. We first determine the mass using the Christodoulou-Ruffini formula and then check its agreement with the result obtained from the surface charge method.

title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
abstract: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

title: Rate-Optimal Spectral Likelihood-Ratio Clustering in Stochastic Block Models
abstract: Spectral clustering commonly assigns communities by clustering a low-dimensional representation, whereas likelihood refinement can improve an initial assignment using the observed edges. We ask whether sharp community-recovery accuracy can be retained when the refinement no longer accesses individual edges. We develop spectral likelihood-ratio clustering for stochastic block models using one regularized adjacency eigensystem and the original vertex degrees. The method estimates connection probabilities and updates each vertex's label by a likelihood-ratio classifier on reconstructed rows. The refinement accepts any sufficiently accurate initialization, including one computed from the same graph. Its expected misclassification proportion is bounded by a constant times the error of a raw-edge oracle classifier, plus the probability that initialization misses the required accuracy. Repeated k-means++ on the retained spectral coordinates supplies one complete procedure with a constant-factor oracle guarantee. The oracle knows the model parameters and the other labels. The guarantee holds for a fixed number of communities, comparable positive block probabilities and community sizes, and a nondegenerate normalized block matrix. It allows arbitrarily slowly diverging expected degrees under the stated upper sparsity condition. We explain the likelihood-ratio construction first, then the regularization and exact-degree correction required by the general result. The proof combines sharp local testing, truncated spectral-row estimates and leave-one-out comparisons.

title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
abstract: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at https://siyingzhao.github.io/BURGER/.

title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese
abstract: Building a language model of one's own no longer requires a data centre. This tutorial trains one from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, and shows how to tell whether it is good for the tasks of a specialist domain. It proposes no new method. It releases a tested Python package and two notebooks in Brazilian Portuguese with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, reference numbers for models of 11 to 12M parameters, and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, at minutes per run, the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs over the same text and then memorises it, while masked diffusion improves up to 256. At their best points on test, the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws and on acts published after training, the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood on the same windows, and it loses to the floor at continuing those acts. It beats the floor at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references more often than the floor and public models of 160M and 630M parameters, only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance, and in filling the blank only when each group weighs the same, since per item it ties the 630M model. On laws, the public models, trained with about 5x10^2 to 10^5 times its compute, lead in tampered text and continuation. The blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.

title: The IRAC Distant Cluster Survey
abstract: We present the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) Distant Cluster Survey (IDCS), a catalog of 825 galaxy cluster and group candidates identified in the Boötes field using the PZWav detection code. Candidates are selected using photometric redshift probability distributions derived from twelve-band optical and infrared imaging. The catalog spans $0.08 < z < 2.0$ (median $z = 0.93$) and includes 147 systems at $z \geq 1.5$. For $z < 1.5$, simulations indicate a purity of $93\%$ at the adopted S/N $\geq 4$ threshold and $50\%$ completeness at $\log(M_{200c}/M_\odot) = 13.74 \pm 0.01$. We validate the cluster photometric redshifts through comparison with spectroscopic data, finding $σ_z/(1+z)=0.017$. Including 18 previously published IRAC Shallow Cluster Survey (ISCS) systems, a total of 80 IDCS cluster candidates are now confirmed through spectroscopy and/or X-ray observations. DESI DR1 spectroscopy provides redshifts for 38 systems, including 23 newly confirmed clusters. These DESI-confirmed systems span $0.12 < z < 0.93$ and have at least 10 spectroscopic members each, from which we measure a median velocity dispersion of $\sim 490$ km s$^{-1}$, corresponding to a median halo mass of $1.1 \times 10^{14} M_\odot$. A positional comparison with 39 independently confirmed literature clusters yields a median centroid offset of 211 kpc. The IDCS catalog provides a cluster sample spanning a wide redshift range, with a selection function characterized through simulations and is a valuable resource for studies of large-scale structure, galaxy evolution in dense environments, and the calibration of cluster detection techniques for current and upcoming wide-field surveys, including LSST, Roman, and Euclid.

title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems.
